Any operating system is likely to run with more processes than the computer has CPUs, so a plan is needed to time-share the CPUs among the processes. Ideally the sharing would be transparent to user processes. A common approach is to provide each process with the illusion that it has its own virtual CPU by multiplexing the processes onto the hardware CPUs. This chapter explains how xv6 achieves this multiplexing.

8.1 Multiplexing

Xv6 multiplexes by switching each CPU from one process to another in two situations. First, xv6 switches when a process makes a system call that blocks (has to wait), for example read or wait. Second, xv6 periodically forces a switch to cope with processes that compute for long periods without blocking. The former are called voluntary switches, the latter involuntary.

Implementing multiplexing poses a few challenges. First, how to switch from one process to another? The basic idea is to save and restore CPU registers, though the fact that this cannot be expressed in C makes it tricky. Second, how to force switches in a way that is transparent to user processes? Xv6 uses the standard technique in which a hardware timer’s interrupts drive context switches. Third, all of the CPUs switch among the same set of processes, so a locking plan is necessary to avoid mistakes such as two CPUs deciding to run the same process at the same time. Fourth, a process’s memory and other resources must be freed when the process exits, but it cannot finish all of this itself. Fifth, each CPU of a multi-core machine must remember which process it is executing so that system calls affect the correct process’s kernel state.

8.2 Context switch overview

The term “context switch” refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption), and resuming execution of a different kernel thread; this switching is the heart of multiplexing. Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process’s kernel thread to another process’s kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU’s “scheduler thread,” and the scheduler thread picks a different process’s kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

At a broader scope, the steps involved in switching from one user process to another are illustrated in Figure 8.1: a trap (system call or interrupt) from the old process’s user space to its kernel thread, a context switch to the current CPU’s scheduler thread, a context switch to a new process’s kernel thread, and a trap return to the user-level process.

8.3 Code: Context switching

The function swtch() in kernel/swtch.S contains the heart of thread context switching: it saves the switched-from thread’s CPU registers, and restores the previously-saved registers of the switched-to thread. The basic reason this is sufficient is that a thread’s state consist of data in memory (e.g. its stack) plus its CPU registers; thread memory need not saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; but the CPU has only one set of registers so they must be switched (saved and restored) between threads.

Each thread’s struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread’s saved registers when it is not running. A CPU’s scheduler thread’s struct context is in that CPU’s struct cpu. When thread X wishes to switch to thread Y, thread X calls swtch(&X’s context, &Y’s context). swtch() saves the current CPU registers in X’s context, then loads the content of Y’s context into the CPU registers, then returns.

swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra,sp,s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers. The RISC-V calling convention requires that if code needs to preserve the value in a caller-saved register across a function call, the compiler must generate instructions that save the register to the stack before the function call, and restore from the stack when the function returns. So swtch can rely on the function that called it having already saved the caller-saved registers (either that, or the calling function didn’t need the values in the registers).

questions.stem:
The following statements summarize how xv6 performs CPU multiplexing and context switching, based on the course material.

1. The term context switch refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption) and resuming execution of a different kernel thread.
2. A thread's state consists of data in memory, such as its stack, plus its CPU registers; different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM, but the CPU has only one set of registers.
3. The function swtch() in kernel/swtch.S saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers and restores the previously saved registers of the switched-to thread.
4. Each thread's struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread's saved registers when it is not running; a CPU's scheduler thread has its struct context in that CPU's struct cpu.
5. Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process's kernel thread to another process's kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread, and the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run and context-switches to that thread.

Based on statements 2 and 3, explain why saving and restoring CPU registers is sufficient for a context switch, and name the registers that swtch() saves. Then, based on statements 1, 4 and 5, describe the role of the scheduler thread in xv6's multiplexing.
questions.answer: Registers must be saved and restored because the CPU has only one set of registers, shared by all threads, while each thread's memory (for example, its stack) stays in a different area of RAM and therefore does not need to be saved or restored during a switch. swtch() saves the callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11) and not the caller-saved registers; the calling function is responsible for having already saved any caller-saved registers it needs across the call. The scheduler thread is the intermediary in xv6's multiplexing: a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's scheduler thread, and the scheduler thread then picks a different process's kernel thread and context-switches to it. Because each thread's saved registers live in its struct context (a process thread's in its struct proc, the scheduler thread's in the CPU's struct cpu), swtch() can save the outgoing thread's registers into its context and load the incoming thread's context into the CPU.
questions.explanation: A context switch saves the outgoing thread's CPU registers into its saved context and loads the incoming thread's saved context into the CPU. Only the registers must be switched because each thread's memory (such as its stack) occupies a separate region of RAM and remains intact. swtch() saves callee-saved registers (ra, sp, s0..s11), relying on the calling function to have preserved caller-saved registers if needed. Xv6 routes switches through the scheduler thread: the outgoing kernel thread switches to the CPU's scheduler thread, which then selects and switches to another process's kernel thread.

response.answer: Saving and restoring CPU registers is sufficient because a thread's complete execution state consists of its memory data (especially its stack) plus its CPU registers. Different threads already keep their memory data in separate areas of RAM, so memory does not need to be copied or swapped during a context switch; only the single hardware register file must be preserved for the outgoing thread and loaded for the incoming thread. swtch() saves the callee-saved registers: ra, sp, s0 through s11. It does not save caller-saved registers because the RISC-V calling convention requires the calling function to save any caller-saved register values it needs across a call, so swtch() can rely on the caller having already preserved them. The scheduler thread in xv6 is the intermediary that enables multiplexing without directly switching from one process's kernel thread to another. When a process's kernel thread gives up the CPU, it context-switches to that CPU's scheduler thread and saves its context in its struct proc. The scheduler thread then selects a different process's kernel thread to run, and context-switches to it using that thread's saved struct context. A CPU's scheduler thread saves its own context in that CPU's struct cpu. Thus the scheduler thread coordinates voluntary and involuntary switches and ensures each CPU resumes the correct kernel thread.

The following excerpts are from course material on xv6 CPU multiplexing.

"The term 'context switch' refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption), and resuming execution of a different kernel thread."

"Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process's kernel thread to another process's kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU's 'scheduler thread,' and the scheduler thread picks a different process's kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread."

"The function swtch() ... saves the switched-from thread's CPU registers, and restores the previously-saved registers of the switched-to thread."

"swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra,sp,s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers."

Using only the excerpts above, answer both parts:

1. State what a context switch preserves during the switch.
2. Describe the scheduler thread's role in xv6's process switching path.

Write a short answer of a few sentences.
questions.answer: A context switch preserves the switched-from kernel thread's CPU registers (callee-saved registers ra, sp, s0..s11) so that execution of that thread can be resumed later, while the switched-to thread's previously saved registers are restored. In xv6, a process's kernel thread does not switch directly to another process's kernel thread; instead it context-switches to that CPU's scheduler thread. The scheduler thread then selects a different process's kernel thread and context-switches to it, so the scheduler thread is the intermediary that chooses which process runs next.

The scheduler thread is the intermediary: a kernel thread gives up the CPU to its CPU's scheduler thread, and that scheduler thread picks another process's kernel thread and switches to it, rather than switching directly process-to-process.

Any operating system is likely to run with more processes than the computer has CPUs, so a plan is needed to time-share the CPUs among the processes. Ideally the sharing would be transparent to user processes. A common approach is to provide each process with the illusion that it has its own virtual CPU by multiplexing the processes onto the hardware CPUs. This chapter explains how xv6 achieves this multiplexing.

8.1 Multiplexing

Xv6 multiplexes by switching each CPU from one process to another in two situations. First, xv6 switches when a process makes a system call that blocks (has to wait), for example read or wait. Second, xv6 periodically forces a switch to cope with processes that compute for long periods without blocking. The former are called voluntary switches, the latter involuntary.

Implementing multiplexing poses a few challenges. First, how to switch from one process to another? The basic idea is to save and restore CPU registers, though the fact that this cannot be expressed in C makes it tricky. Second, how to force switches in a way that is transparent to user processes? Xv6 uses the standard technique in which a hardware timer’s interrupts drive context switches. Third, all of the CPUs switch among the same set of processes, so a locking plan is necessary to avoid mistakes such as two CPUs deciding to run the same process at the same time. Fourth, a process’s memory and other resources must be freed when the process exits, but it cannot finish all of this itself. Fifth, each CPU of a multi-core machine must remember which process it is executing so that system calls affect the correct process’s kernel state.

8.2 Context switch overview

The term “context switch” refers to the steps involved in a CPU leaving off execution of one kernel thread (usually for later resumption), and resuming execution of a different kernel thread; this switching is the heart of multiplexing. Xv6 does not directly context switch from one process’s kernel thread to another process’s kernel thread; instead, a kernel thread gives up the CPU by context-switching to that CPU’s “scheduler thread,” and the scheduler thread picks a different process’s kernel thread to run, and context-switches to that thread.

At a broader scope, the steps involved in switching from one user process to another are illustrated in Figure 8.1: a trap (system call or interrupt) from the old process’s user space to its kernel thread, a context switch to the current CPU’s scheduler thread, a context switch to a new process’s kernel thread, and a trap return to the user-level process.

8.3 Code: Context switching

The function swtch() in kernel/swtch.S contains the heart of thread context switching: it saves the switched-from thread’s CPU registers, and restores the previously-saved registers of the switched-to thread. The basic reason this is sufficient is that a thread’s state consist of data in memory (e.g. its stack) plus its CPU registers; thread memory need not saved and restored because different threads keep their data in different areas of RAM; but the CPU has only one set of registers so they must be switched (saved and restored) between threads.

Each thread’s struct proc includes a struct context that holds the thread’s saved registers when it is not running. A CPU’s scheduler thread’s struct context is in that CPU’s struct cpu. When thread X wishes to switch to thread Y, thread X calls swtch(&X’s context, &Y’s context). swtch() saves the current CPU registers in X’s context, then loads the content of Y’s context into the CPU registers, then returns.

swtch saves callee-saved registers (ra,sp,s0..s11) but not caller-saved registers. The RISC-V calling convention requires that if code needs to preserve the value in a caller-saved register across a function call, the compiler must generate instructions that save the register to the stack before the function call, and restore from the stack when the function returns. So swtch can rely on the function that called it having already saved the caller-saved registers (either that, or the calling function didn’t need the values in the registers).
